title: Πρωτέως Ἅλωσις
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Continuing his tale to Telemachus, Menelaus describes how, disguised in sealskins with three companions, he lay in wait among Proteus's seals at midday and seized the shape-shifting Old Man of the Sea, holding him fast through his transformations into a lion, a serpent, water, and a tree. Once mastered, Proteus tells Menelaus that he must sail back to the Nile and offer hecatombs to the gods before he can reach home. Pressed for news of the other Achaean leaders, Proteus goes on to relate the deaths of two of them on their way home from Troy: Ajax son of Oileus, drowned after a reckless boast defied Poseidon, and Agamemnon, murdered by Aegisthus at a treacherous banquet on his return — a story Proteus has not yet finished telling by this part's end.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δ’ ἄρ’ ἥ γ’ ὑποδῦσα θαλάσσης εὐρέα κόλπον
τέσσαρα φωκάων ἐκ πόντου δέρματ’ ἔνεικε·
sentences.tr:
tophra d’ ar’ hē g’ hypodysa thalassēs eurea kolpon
tessara phōkaōn ek pontou dermat’ eneike·
sentences.l:
Meanwhile she, having dived into the sea’s broad bosom,
brought four sealskins up out of the deep;
sentences.i: Meanwhile Eidothea dove into the broad bosom of the sea and brought up four sealskins from the deep.
sentences.n: ἥ γε picks up Eidothea, unnamed here, continuing the narrative begun in the previous part. ὑποδῦσα is the aorist active participle of ὑποδύω ‘dive under, slip beneath’. κόλπος, literally ‘fold, bosom’, is used here of the broad expanse of the sea, as of a bay. ἔνεικε is the epic aorist of φέρω, from a separate root (ἐνεκ-); whether this form has lost an original augment is uncertain, so no claim is made either way.

sentences.t: πάντα δ’ ἔσαν νεόδαρτα·
sentences.tr: panta d’ esan neodarta·
sentences.l: And all were newly-flayed;
sentences.i: All of them were freshly stripped from the seals;
sentences.n: νεόδαρτα, ‘newly flayed, freshly skinned’ (νέος + δέρω), is a rare compound describing the skins as just taken from the seals. ἔσαν is the epic form of ἦσαν, the imperfect of εἰμί ‘be’; the plural agrees with the neuter plural δέρματα of the line before, an ordinary Greek concord for neuter plurals.

sentences.t: δόλον δ’ ἐπεμήδετο πατρί.
sentences.tr: dolon d’ epemēdeto patri.
sentences.l: and a trick she was devising against her father.
sentences.i: for she was plotting a trick against her own father.
sentences.n: ἐπεμήδετο is the imperfect middle of ἐπιμήδομαι, ‘devise, contrive against’, with the dative πατρί, ‘against her father’. Eidothea is Proteus’s own daughter, and the trick she plots is the ambush to come.

sentences.t:
εὐνὰς δ’ ἐν ψαμάθοισι διαγλάψασ’ ἁλίῃσιν
ἧστο μένουσ’·
sentences.tr:
eunas d’ en psamathoisi diaglapsas’ haliēisin
hēsto menous’·
sentences.l:
And having scooped out lairs in the briny sands,
she sat waiting;
sentences.i: She hollowed out lairs in the briny sand and sat there waiting;
sentences.n: διαγλάψασα, the aorist participle of the rare verb διαγλάφω ‘scoop out, hollow out’, describes digging the hollows where the men will lie hidden. ἁλίῃσιν is an uncontracted dative plural adjective (-ῃσι for Attic -αις) agreeing with ψαμάθοισι. ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit, remain seated’.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς δὲ μάλα σχεδὸν ἤλθομεν αὐτῆς·
sentences.tr: hēmeis de mala schedon ēlthomen autēs·
sentences.l: and we came very close to her;
sentences.i: and we came up quite close to her side;
sentences.n: σχεδόν, ‘near, close by’, takes the genitive αὐτῆς, ‘of her’, a construction of the adverb acting almost like a preposition. μάλα strengthens it further, ‘very close’. ἤλθομεν is the 1st plural aorist of ἔρχομαι, describing Menelaus and his three companions approaching Eidothea where she waited among the dug-out lairs.

sentences.t: ἑξείης δ’ εὔνησε, βάλεν δ’ ἐπὶ δέρμα ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.tr: hexeiēs d’ eunēse, balen d’ epi derma hekastōi.
sentences.l: and in a row she laid us down, and threw a skin over each one.
sentences.i: She laid us down in a row and threw a sealskin over each of us.
sentences.n: ἑξείης, ‘in order, in a row’, recurs of the seals themselves at 449. εὔνησε is the causative aorist of εὐνάω, ‘lay to rest’. βάλεν is an unaugmented aorist of βάλλω (Attic ἔβαλε).

sentences.t: ἔνθα κεν αἰνότατος λόχος ἔπλετο·
sentences.tr: entha ken ainotatos lochos epleto·
sentences.l: There indeed would the ambush have been most dreadful;
sentences.i: That would have been the most dreadful ambush of all;
sentences.n: κεν with the aorist indicative ἔπλετο (from πέλομαι, ‘be, become’) makes a past potential, ‘would have been’. αἰνότατος is the superlative of αἰνός, ‘dreadful’, echoed by the adverb αἰνῶς later in the same line. λόχος, ‘ambush’, shares its root with λοχησάμενος, ‘having lain in ambush’, which Proteus himself uses of this same ambush at 4.463.

sentences.t:
τεῖρε γὰρ αἰνῶς
φωκάων ἁλιοτρεφέων ὀλοώτατος ὀδμή·
sentences.tr:
teire gar ainōs
phōkaōn haliotrepheōn oloōtatos odmē·
sentences.l:
for terribly wore-us-down
the most deadly smell of the sea-bred seals;
sentences.i: for the deadly smell of the sea-bred seals wore us down terribly;
sentences.n: τεῖρε is the imperfect of τείρω, ‘wear down, distress’. ἁλιοτρεφέων, ‘sea-bred, sea-nurtured’ (ἅλς + τρέφω), is a rare compound; its formation is transparent from ἅλς and τρέφω even though the word is otherwise unattested in this part. ὀλοώτατος is the superlative of ὀλοός ‘deadly, destructive’, the same adjective behind Ἄτλαντος ὀλοόφρονος (1.52).

sentences.t: τίς γάρ κ’ εἰναλίῳ παρὰ κήτεϊ κοιμηθείη;
sentences.tr: tis gar k’ einaliōi para kēteï koimētheiē;
sentences.l: For who could sleep beside a monster of the sea?
sentences.i: For who could bear to sleep next to a creature of the sea?
sentences.n: κ(ε) with the optative κοιμηθείη makes a potential question, ‘who could...?’. κῆτος is properly any huge sea-creature or ‘monster’; used loosely here of the seals themselves, for rhetorical effect.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ αὐτὴ ἐσάωσε καὶ ἐφράσατο μέγ’ ὄνειαρ·
sentences.tr: all’ autē esaōse kai ephrasato meg’ oneiar·
sentences.l: But she herself saved us, and devised a great remedy;
sentences.i: But she herself came to our rescue and thought of a great help;
sentences.n: αὐτή is Eidothea. ἐσάωσε is the aorist of σαόω ‘save’ (the same verb recurs of Hera at 513). ἐφράσατο is the aorist middle of φράζομαι, ‘devise, think of’ (recurring of Aegisthus’s plot at 529). ὄνειαρ, ‘help, remedy, boon’, is a neuter noun of the same root as ὀνίνημι ‘benefit’.

sentences.t:
ἀμβροσίην ὑπὸ ῥῖνα ἑκάστῳ θῆκε φέρουσα
ἡδὺ μάλα πνείουσαν, ὄλεσσε δὲ κήτεος ὀδμήν.
sentences.tr:
ambrosiēn hypo rhina hekastōi thēke pherousa
hēdy mala pneiousan, olesse de kēteos odmēn.
sentences.l:
Ambrosia beneath the nose of each she placed, bringing it,
breathing very sweetly, and it destroyed the monster’s smell.
sentences.i: She brought ambrosia, sweet-smelling, and placed it beneath each man’s nose, and it destroyed the stench of the sea-creature.
sentences.n: ἀμβροσίη, ‘ambrosia’, the fragrant divine substance, is used here almost like a perfume. θῆκε is the aorist of τίθημι. ὄλεσσε is an unaugmented aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’ (Attic ὤλεσε). κήτεος repeats the noun of line 443.

sentences.t: πᾶσαν δ’ ἠοίην μένομεν τετληότι θυμῷ·
sentences.tr: pasan d’ ēoiēn menomen tetlēoti thymōi·
sentences.l: And all the morning we waited with enduring heart;
sentences.i: All through the morning we waited with enduring hearts;
sentences.n: πᾶσαν...ἠοίην, ‘the whole morning’, is an accusative of duration. μένομεν has past force in this narrative context, though its form does not itself distinguish present from unaugmented imperfect. τετληότι θυμῷ, ‘with an enduring heart’, is the perfect participle of τλάω used distributively for the whole group (compare the singular-for-plural ἦτορ ἑταίρων, 4.374); it recurs unchanged at 459 and keeps the same English both times.

sentences.t: φῶκαι δ’ ἐξ ἁλὸς ἦλθον ἀολλέες.
sentences.tr: phōkai d’ ex halos ēlthon aollees.
sentences.l: And the seals came from the sea, thronging together.
sentences.i: Then the seals came in from the sea, all together in a throng.
sentences.n: ἀολλέες, ‘in a body, thronging together’, is the adjective ἀολλής, describing the seals as they come ashore all at once from the sea. ἦλθον is the aorist of ἔρχομαι. This unit marks the moment the ambush’s real danger begins, as the men lie hidden among the animals whose smell Eidothea’s ambrosia has just made bearable to them.

sentences.t:
αἱ μὲν ἔπειτα
ἑξῆς εὐνάζοντο παρὰ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης·
sentences.tr:
hai men epeita
hexēs eunazonto para rhēgmini thalassēs·
sentences.l:
They then, one after another,
lay down to rest along the surf-line of the sea;
sentences.i: and then, one after another, they lay down to rest along the breaking surf of the sea;
sentences.n: ἑξῆς, ‘in a row, in order’, echoes ἑξείης at 440. εὐνάζοντο is an imperfect middle, ‘were bedding themselves down’. παρὰ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης, ‘along the surf-line of the sea’, varies only the preposition of the same collocation used with ἐπί at 4.430 (odyssey-017), shipped there as ‘upon the surf-line of the sea’; the English preposition follows the Greek one (παρά ‘along, beside’ there ἐπί ‘upon, at’).

sentences.t:
ἔνδιος δ’ ὁ γέρων ἦλθ’ ἐξ ἁλός, εὗρε δὲ φώκας
ζατρεφέας, πάσας δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπῴχετο, λέκτο δ’ ἀριθμόν·
sentences.tr:
endios d’ ho gerōn ēlth’ ex halos, heure de phōkas
zatrepheas, pasas d’ ar’ epōicheto, lekto d’ arithmon·
sentences.l:
And at midday the old man came from the sea, and found the sleek seals,
and went along all of them, and counted their number;
sentences.i: At midday the old man came up from the sea and found the well-fed seals; he went along all of them and counted them off;
sentences.n: ὁ γέρων, the bare ‘the old man’, is used here of Proteus for the first time in this part; the same plain rendering is already established for a figure who has been given his fuller epithets earlier (compare ὁ γέρων/ὁ γεραιός of Nestor, 3.373 etc.), and is kept consistent here — see new-renderings.md. ἔνδιος, ‘at midday’, is used adverbially. ζατρεφέας, ‘well-fed, sleek’ (ζα- intensive + τρέφω), is a rare compound, its formation transparent from the intensive prefix ζα- on τρέφω. λέκτο, the aorist middle of λέγω ‘count’, is distinct in sense from the identically formed λέκτο of λέχομαι ‘lie down’ at 453.

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἡμέας πρώτους λέγε κήτεσιν, οὐδέ τι θυμῷ
ὠΐσθη δόλον εἶναι·
sentences.tr:
en d’ hēmeas prōtous lege kētesin, oude ti thymōi
ōïsthē dolon einai·
sentences.l:
And among the monsters he counted us first, nor at all in his heart
did he suspect there was a trick;
sentences.i: He counted us first among the sea-beasts, and had no idea in his heart that there was a trick;
sentences.n: κήτεσιν, ‘among the sea-creatures’, repeats the word of line 443, now applied to the seals themselves as Proteus counts them, with the disguised men among them. ὠΐσθη is an uncontracted aorist passive (deponent) of ὀΐομαι, ‘suppose, suspect’.

sentences.t: ἔπειτα δὲ λέκτο καὶ αὐτός.
sentences.tr: epeita de lekto kai autos.
sentences.l: and then he too lay down himself.
sentences.i: and then he himself lay down to rest.
sentences.n: λέκτο here is the aorist middle of λέχομαι, ‘lie down to rest’ — a different verb from the identically spelled λέκτο of λέγω ‘count’ at line 451; the poet’s repetition of the same form for two different verbs is a genuine wordplay, not an error.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ ἰάχοντες ἐπεσσύμεθ’, ἀμφὶ δὲ χεῖρας
βάλλομεν·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis de iachontes epessymeth’, amphi de cheiras
ballomen·
sentences.l:
And we, shouting, rushed upon him, and around him our hands
we threw;
sentences.i: Then we rushed at him with a shout, and threw our arms around him;
sentences.n: ἰάχοντες is the present participle of ἰάχω, ‘shout, cry out’. ἐπεσσύμεθα, from ἐπισεύομαι, is a middle perfect used with present force, ‘we rushed upon’. ἀμφὶ...βάλλομεν is tmesis for ἀμφιβάλλομεν, ‘throw around, embrace’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὁ γέρων δολίης ἐπελήθετο τέχνης,
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι πρώτιστα λέων γένετ’ ἠυγένειος,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα δράκων καὶ πάρδαλις ἠδὲ μέγας σῦς·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ho gerōn doliēs epelētheto technēs,
all’ ē toi prōtista leōn genet’ ēygeneios,
autar epeita drakōn kai pardalis ēde megas sys·
sentences.i: But the old man did not forget his guileful device: first of all he turned into a well-maned lion, then a serpent, a leopard, and a huge boar;
sentences.n: δολίης...τέχνης, ‘guileful device’, is kept to the same English used of Aegisthus’s plot at 529 (δολίην...τέχνην); the repetition of the identical phrase for Proteus’s shape-shifting and for Aegisthus’s murder-plot links the two figures deliberately, and the choice to render both alike is recorded in new-renderings.md. ἠυγένειος, ‘well-maned’ (literally ‘with a fine chin/beard’), describes the lion. γένετ(ο) is an unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι.

sentences.t: γίγνετο δ’ ὑγρὸν ὕδωρ καὶ δένδρεον ὑψιπέτηλον·
sentences.tr: gigneto d’ hygron hydōr kai dendreon hypsipetēlon·
sentences.l: and he became flowing water, and a high-leaved tree;
sentences.i: then he turned into flowing water, and a tall, leafy tree;
sentences.n: γίγνετο, an imperfect, marks the whole cycling series of transformations as ongoing, in contrast to the aorist γένετ(ο) that opened the sequence at 456. ὑψιπέτηλον, ‘high-leaved, tall-leaved’ (ὑψι- + πέταλον ‘leaf’), describes the tree-shape, the last and strangest of Proteus’s disguises before he gives up the struggle.

sentences.t: ἡμεῖς δ’ ἀστεμφέως ἔχομεν τετληότι θυμῷ.
sentences.tr: hēmeis d’ astempheōs echomen tetlēoti thymōi.
sentences.l: but we held on unyieldingly with enduring heart.
sentences.i: But we held on unyieldingly, with enduring hearts.
sentences.n: ἀστεμφέως, ‘unyieldingly, without flinching’, is an adverb from ἀστεμφής. τετληότι θυμῷ repeats line 447 verbatim and keeps the identical English both times, as a recurring phrase should.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἀνίαζ’ ὁ γέρων ὀλοφώια εἰδώς,
καὶ τότε δή μ’ ἐπέεσσιν ἀνειρόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ aniaz’ ho gerōn olophōia eidōs,
kai tote dē m’ epeessin aneiromenos proseeipe·
sentences.l:
But when indeed the old man, knowing baneful wiles, grew weary,
then indeed he addressed me with words, asking:
sentences.i: But when at last the old man, for all his baneful tricks, grew weary, he spoke to me and asked:
sentences.n: ἀνίαζε is the imperfect of ἀνιάζω, ‘be distressed, grow weary’. ὀλοφώια, ‘baneful tricks’, is the same substantival neuter plural already fixed at 4.410 (odyssey-017) of Proteus’s shape-shifting, reused here unchanged. ἀνειρόμενος is the present participle of ἀνείρομαι, ‘ask, inquire’. This unit is narration introducing Proteus’s first speech; the mark and the opening quotation mark belong to the next unit, not to this one.

sentences.t:
τίς νύ τοι, Ἀτρέος υἱέ, θεῶν συμφράσσατο βουλάς,
ὄφρα μ’ ἕλοις ἀέκοντα λοχησάμενος;
sentences.tr:
tis ny toi, Atreos huie, theōn symphrassato boulas,
ophra m’ helois aekonta lochēsamenos;
sentences.l:
“Who now, son of Atreus, of the gods planned counsels with you,
so that lying in wait you might take me unwilling?
sentences.i: “Which of the gods, son of Atreus, plotted this plan with you, so that you might lie in wait and catch me against my will?
sentences.n: This is Proteus’s first speech in the whole poem, so it opens with a fresh top-level quotation mark, on the pattern of Eidothea’s first speech at 4.371 (odyssey-017). συμφράσσατο, ‘planned together, contrived with’, takes βουλάς as its object and an implied ‘with you’. ἀέκοντα, ‘unwilling’, agrees with the unexpressed ‘me’, object of ἕλοις. λοχησάμενος is the aorist participle of λοχάομαι, ‘lie in ambush’ — the same root as λόχος at line 441.

sentences.t: τέο σε χρή;
sentences.tr: teo se chrē;
sentences.l: What do you need?”
sentences.i: What is it that you need?”
sentences.n: τέο is the Homeric/Ionic genitive interrogative pronoun (= Attic τίνος), used here with the impersonal χρή, literally ‘of what is there need to you?’. This closes Proteus’s first speech, hence the closing mark; Menelaus’s own recalled reply begins at the next unit.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, autar egō min ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: This exact reply-formula (ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·) already stands published word for word as odyssey-017’s unit at line 375, where it reported Menelaus answering Eidothea, and the build’s mechanical reuse rule requires the identical English here too. μιν and the 3rd-singular ἔφατ(ο) are grammatically gender-neutral in Greek; the pronouns ‘she’/‘her’ in this shipped English describe Eidothea in that earlier, unrelated context, not Proteus, who is in fact the person Menelaus is answering here — a reader should not take ‘her’ to mean Proteus.

sentences.t: οἶσθα, γέρον, τί με ταῦτα παρατροπέων ἐρεείνεις;
sentences.tr: oistha, geron, ti me tauta paratropeōn ereeineis;
sentences.l: ‘You know, old man, why do you question me about this, turning me aside from my purpose?
sentences.i: ‘You know well, old man, why do you question me about this, trying to lead me astray?
sentences.n: οἶσθα is the 2nd singular perfect of οἶδα, with present force, ‘you know’. παρατροπέων, the present participle of παρατροπέω, ‘turn aside, put off with evasions’, pictures Proteus trying to distract Menelaus from his real question. ἐρεείνεις is the epic long form (= ἐρωτᾷς) of the verb ‘ask, question’. This opens Menelaus’s own recalled reply, a speech nested within his outer narration, marked with its own single quotation mark.
sentences.mark: Menelaus recalls his answer to Proteus

sentences.t:
ὡς δὴ δήθ’ ἐνὶ νήσῳ ἐρύκομαι, οὐδέ τι τέκμωρ
εὑρέμεναι δύναμαι, μινύθει δέ μοι ἔνδοθεν ἦτορ.
sentences.tr:
hōs dē dēth’ eni nēsōi erykomai, oude ti tekmōr
heuremenai dynamai, minythei de moi endothen ētor.
sentences.l:
seeing that for so long now on the island I am held back, nor at all an end
am I able to find, and within me my heart wastes away.
sentences.i: since I am held so long on this island, unable to find any way out of it, while my heart wastes away within me.
sentences.n: This closely echoes the almost identical line Eidothea herself had spoken to Menelaus at 4.373–374 (odyssey-017), ‘ἐνὶ νήσῳ ἐρύκεαι...μινύθει δέ τοι ἦτορ ἑταίρων’ (‘you are held...the heart of your companions wastes away’); Menelaus now repeats the same complaint in the 1st person and about his own heart (ἔνδοθεν ἦτορ) rather than his companions’. τέκμωρ, ‘a fixed limit, an end’, and εὑρέμεναι, an infinitive in -έμεναι (Attic εὑρεῖν), are the same words used there.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ πέρ μοι εἰπέ, θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα ἴσασιν,
ὅς τίς μ’ ἀθανάτων πεδάᾳ καὶ ἔδησε κελεύθου,
νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσομαι ἰχθυόεντα.
sentences.tr:
alla sy per moi eipe, theoi de te panta isasin,
hos tis m’ athanatōn pedaāi kai edēse keleuthou,
noston th’, hōs epi ponton eleusomai ichthyoenta.
sentences.l:
But you, for your part, tell me — and the gods know all things —
which of the immortals fetters me and has bound me from my path,
and of my return, how I shall come upon the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.i: But you at least tell me — since the gods know everything — which of the immortals holds me fettered and has barred my way, and how I am to make my way home across the fish-teeming sea.’
sentences.n: This whole unit is byte-for-byte identical, across all three lines, to the unit already published at odyssey-017’s line 379, where Menelaus spoke the same words to Eidothea; the build’s reuse rule requires the identical shipped English here, including the closing ’ that ends this recalled speech to Proteus exactly as it did the recalled speech to Eidothea. νόστον θ’, ὡς ἐπὶ πόντον ἐλεύσομαι ἰχθυόεντα is the already-fixed formula ‘and of my return, how I shall come upon the fish-teeming sea’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, ho de m’ autik’ ameibomenos proseeipen·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:
sentences.i: So I said, and he answered me at once:
sentences.n: This reply-formula is new in the poem so far and is fixed here as a new house rendering, since it recurs unchanged at line 491 later in this same part — see new-renderings.md. ὁ here is explicitly masculine, ‘he’, referring to Proteus, unlike the gender-neutral formula reused at 464. ἐφάμην is the imperfect middle 1st singular of φημί.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ὤφελλες Διί τ’ ἄλλοισίν τε θεοῖσι
ῥέξας ἱερὰ κάλ’ ἀναβαινέμεν, ὄφρα τάχιστα
σὴν ἐς πατρίδ’ ἵκοιο πλέων ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον.
sentences.tr:
alla mal’ ōphelles Dii t’ alloisin te theoisi
rhexas hiera kal’ anabainemen, ophra tachista
sēn es patrid’ hikoio pleōn epi oinopa ponton.
sentences.l:
“But you ought indeed, to Zeus and to the other gods
having offered fair sacrifices, to have gone aboard, so that most quickly
to your own fatherland you might come, sailing over the wine-faced open-sea.
sentences.i: “You ought indeed to have offered fair sacrifices to Zeus and the other gods and then gone aboard your ship, so that you might come most quickly to your own fatherland, sailing over the sea that has the look of wine.
sentences.n: ὤφελλες with the infinitive ἀναβαινέμεν is the regular Homeric idiom for a missed past obligation, ‘you ought to have...’, built on the imperfect of ὀφείλω without ἄν. ῥέξας is the aorist participle of ῥέζω, ‘perform (a sacrifice)’. ἀναβαινέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν of ἀναβαίνω, ‘go aboard, embark’. οἴνοψ πόντος is the already-fixed epithet, ‘the wine-faced open-sea’. This opens Proteus’s second speech, reopening his own top-level quotation mark after the intervening narration.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τοι πρὶν μοῖρα φίλους τ’ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι
οἶκον ἐυκτίμενον καὶ σὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
sentences.tr:
ou gar toi prin moira philous t’ ideein kai hikesthai
oikon eyktimenon kai sēn es patrida gaian,
sentences.l:
For it is not your fate before that to see your dear ones and to reach
your well-built home and your own fatherland,
sentences.i: For it is not fated for you to see your dear ones or to reach your well-built home and your own native land before that,
sentences.n: μοῖρα, with an understood ἐστί, ‘it is fate/destiny’, governs the infinitives ἰδέειν and ἱκέσθαι. πρίν here looks ahead to πρίν γ’ ὅτ’ ἄν in the next unit, ‘not...until’. ἐυκτίμενον, ‘well-built’, is the already-fixed epithet (compare ἐυκτίμενον πτολίεθρον, 3.4), here applied to Menelaus’s own house.

sentences.t:
πρίν γ’ ὅτ’ ἂν Αἰγύπτοιο, διιπετέος ποταμοῖο,
αὖτις ὕδωρ ἔλθῃς ῥέξῃς θ’ ἱερὰς ἑκατόμβας
ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι·
sentences.tr:
prin g’ hot’ an Aigyptoio, diipeteos potamoio,
autis hydōr elthēis rhexēis th’ hieras hekatombas
athanatoisi theoisi, toi ouranon euryn echousi·
sentences.i: until you come back to the waters of Egypt, the river fallen from the sky, and offer sacred hecatombs to the immortal gods who hold the broad heaven;
sentences.n: διιπετέος, ‘fallen from the sky’ (Διός + πίπτω), is a standing epithet of great rivers, here of the Nile (‘Egypt’), pictured as fed from above by Zeus’s rain. Αἰγύπτοιο is a genitive in -οιο. ἔλθῃς and ῥέξῃς are subjunctives with ἄν in an indefinite temporal clause, ‘until you come...and offer’. τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι repeats the standing periphrasis for the gods already fixed at 1.65–67.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε τοι δώσουσιν ὁδὸν θεοί, ἣν σὺ μενοινᾷς.
sentences.tr: kai tote toi dōsousin hodon theoi, hēn sy menoināis.
sentences.l: and then indeed the gods will grant you the way that you desire.”
sentences.i: and then the gods will grant you the journey you long for.”
sentences.n: δώσουσιν is a plain future, ‘will give, grant’. μενοινᾷς, ‘you long for, desire eagerly’ (μενοινάω), is present. This closes Proteus’s second speech; both layers end with the closing mark.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐμοί γε κατεκλάσθη φίλον ἦτορ,
οὕνεκά μ’ αὖτις ἄνωγεν ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον
Αἴγυπτόνδ’ ἰέναι, δολιχὴν ὁδὸν ἀργαλέην τε.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’, autar emoi ge kateklasthē philon ētor,
houneka m’ autis anōgen ep’ ēeroeidea ponton
Aigyptond’ ienai, dolichēn hodon argaleēn te.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and my own heart was broken within me,
because he bade me go again over the misty-looking sea
to Egypt, a long and grievous way.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and my heart was broken within me, because he was bidding me go back again across the misty-looking sea to Egypt, a long and grievous journey.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ(ο), ‘so he spoke’, is the fixed closing formula for a speech. κατεκλάσθη, an aorist passive of κατακλάω ‘break down, shatter’, pictures the heart as physically crushed by despair. ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον is the already-fixed ‘the misty-looking sea’; ἀργαλέην, ‘grievous’, is the same adjective already fixed in μνηστὺς ἀργαλέη.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὣς μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.tr: alla kai hōs mythoisin ameibomenos proseeipon·
sentences.l: But even so, in words, answering, I addressed him:
sentences.i: But even so I answered him and said:
sentences.n: μύθοισιν, a dative plural of μῦθος, is instrumental, ‘with words’. ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is a 1st-person variant of the reply-formulas already fixed for the 3rd person elsewhere in the poem. This is plain narration leading into Menelaus’s third reply, with no mark of its own.

sentences.t: ταῦτα μὲν οὕτω δὴ τελέω, γέρον, ὡς σὺ κελεύεις.
sentences.tr: tauta men houtō dē teleō, geron, hōs sy keleueis.
sentences.l: ‘These things, then, thus indeed I will accomplish, old man, as you bid.
sentences.i: ‘These things, then, I will certainly carry out, old man, just as you command.
sentences.n: τελέω is a future, ‘I will accomplish, fulfil’, with ταῦτα (‘these things’) as its object, referring to the sacrifices and voyage Proteus has just prescribed. κελεύεις is present, ‘you command, bid’. γέρον, vocative, is kept to the same rendering, ‘old man’, already used at 465.
sentences.mark: Menelaus recalls his second answer to Proteus

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
sentences.tr: all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon,
sentences.l: But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly;
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly:
sentences.n: This whole line is already fixed in the house-rendering table and already shipped byte-for-byte at odyssey-002’s unit at line 169; the identical English is reused here. It continues Menelaus’s own recalled speech, already open, so no new mark or quotation mark is needed.

sentences.t:
ἢ πάντες σὺν νηυσὶν ἀπήμονες ἦλθον Ἀχαιοί,
οὓς Νέστωρ καὶ ἐγὼ λίπομεν Τροίηθεν ἰόντες,
ἦέ τις ὤλετ’ ὀλέθρῳ ἀδευκέι ἧς ἐπὶ νηὸς
ἠὲ φίλων ἐν χερσίν, ἐπεὶ πόλεμον τολύπευσεν.
sentences.tr:
ē pantes syn nēusin apēmones ēlthon Achaioi,
hous Nestōr kai egō lipomen Troiēthen iontes,
ēe tis ōlet’ olethrōi adeukei hēs epi nēos
ēe philōn en chersin, epei polemon tolypeusen.
sentences.l:
whether all the Achaeans came home unharmed with their ships,
whom Nestor and I left, going from Troy,
or whether someone perished by a bitter doom upon his own ship
or in the arms of his friends, after he had wound up the war.’
sentences.i: whether all the Achaeans, whom Nestor and I left behind as we set out from Troy, came home safe with their ships, or whether one of them perished by a bitter doom on his own ship, or in the arms of his friends, once he had wound up the war.’
sentences.n: ἀπήμονες, ‘unharmed, unscathed’, recurs at 519 of Agamemnon’s own homecoming. Τροίηθεν, ‘from Troy’, carries the directional suffix -θεν. ἀδευκέι, ‘bitter, harsh’, is a rare adjective of uncertain further derivation, glossed ‘bitter’ since antiquity. The closing half-line, ἠὲ φίλων ἐν χερσίν, ἐπεὶ πόλεμον τολύπευσεν, repeats word for word the close of the unit already published at odyssey-003’s line 235, and its shipped wording, ‘or in the arms of his friends, after he had wound up the war’, is reused for that half-line, though the rest of this new sentence is freshly rendered, since only the final half-line repeats. This closes Menelaus’s third recalled reply.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.tr: hōs ephamēn, ho de m’ autik’ ameibomenos proseeipen·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:
sentences.i: So I said, and he answered me at once:
sentences.n: This line is word for word identical to line 471 earlier in this same part, where this reply-formula was fixed as a new house rendering; the identical English is repeated here, as the rule for a recurring line requires.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη, τί με ταῦτα διείρεαι;
sentences.tr: Atreïdē, ti me tauta dieireai;
sentences.l: “Son of Atreus, why do you question me about these things?
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, why do you ask me about this?
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη, vocative, is the fixed periphrasis ‘son of Atreus’, used elsewhere of both sons of Atreus, Menelaus and Agamemnon, with context deciding which (compare Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, 4.156, and Ἀτρεΐδης used alone of Agamemnon, 3.193); here it addresses Menelaus. διείρεαι is the present middle 2nd singular of διέρομαι, an intensive of ἔρομαι, ‘ask closely about’. This opens Proteus’s third and final speech in this part, reopening his own quotation mark.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
ἴδμεναι, οὐδὲ δαῆναι ἐμὸν νόον·
sentences.tr:
oude ti se chrē
idmenai, oude daēnai emon noon·
sentences.l:
Nor is there any need for you
to know it, nor to learn my mind;
sentences.i: There is no need at all for you to know it, or to learn my mind;
sentences.n: ἴδμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι of οἶδα (= Attic εἰδέναι), ‘to know’. δαῆναι, an aorist infinitive, ‘to learn’, shares its root with the disputed δαΐφρων (1.48).

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σέ φημι
δὴν ἄκλαυτον ἔσεσθαι, ἐπὴν ἐὺ πάντα πύθηαι.
sentences.tr:
oude se phēmi
dēn aklauton esesthai, epēn ey panta pythēai.
sentences.l:
nor do I say that you
will long be without tears, once you have learned everything well.
sentences.i: nor do I think that you will long be free of tears, once you have heard the whole of it clearly.
sentences.n: φημί with the accusative and infinitive gives ‘I do not say/think that...’. ἄκλαυτον, ‘without weeping’ (ἀ- + κλαίω), is a predicate adjective. πύθηαι is an aorist subjunctive of πυνθάνομαι, ‘learn, hear of’, with the epic ending -ηαι (Attic πύθῃ), after ἐπήν (= ἐπεὶ ἄν) ‘once, whenever’.

sentences.t: πολλοὶ μὲν γὰρ τῶν γε δάμεν, πολλοὶ δὲ λίποντο·
sentences.tr: polloi men gar tōn ge damen, polloi de liponto·
sentences.l: For many indeed of them were slain, but many were left;
sentences.i: For many of them were killed, but many survived;
sentences.n: δάμεν is an unaugmented aorist passive of δαμάζω, ‘subdue, kill’ (Attic ἐδάμησαν). λίποντο, an aorist middle of λείπω used passively in sense, ‘were left behind, survived’.

sentences.t:
ἀρχοὶ δ’ αὖ δύο μοῦνοι Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων
ἐν νόστῳ ἀπόλοντο·
sentences.tr:
archoi d’ au dyo mounoi Achaiōn chalkochitōnōn
en nostōi apolonto·
sentences.l:
And of leaders, again, only two of the bronze-shirted Achaeans
perished on their homeward way;
sentences.i: But of their leaders, only two of the bronze-shirted Achaeans perished on the way home;
sentences.n: μοῦνοι, ‘only, alone’, is the Ionic form of μόνοι. Ἀχαιῶν χαλκοχιτώνων is the already-fixed epithet ‘the bronze-shirted Achaeans’. ἀπόλοντο is an unaugmented aorist middle of ἀπόλλυμι.

sentences.t: μάχῃ δέ τε καὶ σὺ παρῆσθα.
sentences.tr: machēi de te kai sy parēstha.
sentences.l: and in the battle you too were present.
sentences.i: and you yourself were there in the fighting.
sentences.n: παρῆσθα is the 2nd singular imperfect of πάρειμι, ‘be present’ (παρά- prefixed to ἦσθα, the ordinary imperfect of εἰμί, identical in Attic); this -σθα is not the distinct epic subjunctive ending that extends -ῃς to -ῃσθα, as in ἐθέλῃσθα, 4.391 (odyssey-017). Proteus notes that Menelaus, unlike Proteus himself, was an eyewitness at Troy and so already knows at first hand how the fighting there went, before Proteus turns to what befell the leaders on the way home.

sentences.t: εἷς δ’ ἔτι που ζωὸς κατερύκεται εὐρέι πόντῳ.
sentences.tr: heis d’ eti pou zōos kateryketai eurei pontōi.
sentences.l: and one is still, I think, held alive somewhere on the broad sea.
sentences.i: and one man is still, I believe, kept alive somewhere out on the wide sea.
sentences.n: κατερύκεται is present passive, ‘is held/detained back’. που, ‘somewhere, I suppose’, marks Proteus’s own uncertainty. This unnamed man is Odysseus, already shown in the poem’s opening (1.13–15, odyssey-001) to be held on Calypso’s island; Proteus does not name him here.

sentences.t: Αἴας μὲν μετὰ νηυσὶ δάμη δολιχηρέτμοισι.
sentences.tr: Aias men meta nēusi damē dolichēretmoisi.
sentences.l: Ajax perished among the long-oared ships.
sentences.i: Ajax met his death among the long-oared ships.
sentences.n: This unit begins a new paragraph in Murray’s text, turning to Ajax’s story, but it remains inside Proteus’s still-open third speech begun at 492, so it carries no mark and no quotation-reopening character — exactly as the corresponding paragraph-break inside an open speech at odyssey-017’s unit at line 351. δάμη is an unaugmented aorist passive of δαμάζω, as at 495. δολιχηρέτμοισι, ‘long-oared’ (δολιχός + ἐρετμόν), is a new epithet in this part, describing the Achaean fleet generally rather than Ajax’s own ship — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
Γυρῇσίν μιν πρῶτα Ποσειδάων ἐπέλασσεν
πέτρῃσιν μεγάλῃσι καὶ ἐξεσάωσε θαλάσσης·
sentences.tr:
Gyrēisin min prōta Poseidaōn epelassen
petrēisin megalēisi kai exesaōse thalassēs·
sentences.l:
Onto the great Gyraean rocks Poseidon first drove him,
and saved him out of the sea;
sentences.i: Poseidon first drove him onto the great Gyraean rocks, and brought him safe out of the sea;
sentences.n: Γυρῇσιν...πέτρῃσιν μεγάλῃσι, ‘the great Gyraean rocks’, names a place whose exact location was already disputed in antiquity and remains unidentified; the name is kept as a transliterated proper name rather than resolved to a guess — see new-renderings.md. ἐπέλασσεν is the aorist of πελάζω, ‘bring near, drive against’. ἐξεσάωσε, ‘saved out of’, is a compound of the σαόω already seen at 444.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν ἔκφυγε κῆρα καὶ ἐχθόμενός περ Ἀθήνῃ,
εἰ μὴ ὑπερφίαλον ἔπος ἔκβαλε καὶ μέγ’ ἀάσθη·
sentences.tr:
kai ny ken ekphyge kēra kai echthomenos per Athēnēi,
ei mē hyperphialon epos ekbale kai meg’ aasthē·
sentences.l:
And now indeed he would have escaped his fate, hated though he was by Athena,
had he not cast out an overweening word, and been greatly blinded;
sentences.i: And he would have escaped his doom then, hated as he was by Athena, had he not let slip an arrogant boast and been struck with a great blindness of mind;
sentences.n: κε with the aorist ἔκφυγε makes a past unreal potential, ‘would have escaped’. ἐχθόμενος, a participle of ἔχθομαι ‘be hated’, takes the dative Ἀθήνῃ. ὑπερφίαλον ἔπος, ‘an overweening word’, names the boast to come. ἀάσθη, ‘was blinded, was infatuated’ (from ἀάω, the root behind the goddess Ἄτη), recurs verbatim at line 509 of this same reckless moment, and the same English, ‘greatly blinded’/‘a great blindness of mind’, is kept for it both times — see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t: φῆ ῥ’ ἀέκητι θεῶν φυγέειν μέγα λαῖτμα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr: phē rh’ aekēti theōn phygeein mega laitma thalassēs.
sentences.l: he declared that in despite of the gods he had escaped the great gulf of the sea.
sentences.i: He boasted that he had escaped the great gulf of the sea in defiance of the gods.
sentences.n: φῆ (= ἔφη) with the infinitive φυγέειν is indirect statement, not a direct quotation, so this unit carries no mark and no quotation marks, unlike the direct speeches elsewhere in this part. ἀέκητι θεῶν, ‘against the will of the gods’, repeats the phrase already used at 1.79. λαῖτμα, ‘the gulf, the deep’, is a poetic word for the sea’s vast expanse.

sentences.t: τοῦ δὲ Ποσειδάων μεγάλ’ ἔκλυεν αὐδήσαντος·
sentences.tr: tou de Poseidaōn megal’ eklyen audēsantos·
sentences.l: And Poseidon heard him greatly, as he cried aloud;
sentences.i: Poseidon heard him plainly as he shouted this;
sentences.n: μεγάλ(α) is an adverbial accusative, ‘loudly, clearly’ (with ἔκλυεν). αὐδήσαντος, a genitive aorist participle of αὐδάω ‘cry out, speak aloud’, agrees with τοῦ, the genitive of the person heard, the regular construction with κλύω.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα τρίαιναν ἑλὼν χερσὶ στιβαρῇσιν
ἤλασε Γυραίην πέτρην, ἀπὸ δ’ ἔσχισεν αὐτήν·
sentences.tr:
autik’ epeita triainan helōn chersi stibarēisin
ēlase Gyraiēn petrēn, apo d’ eschisen autēn·
sentences.l:
At once then, taking his trident in his sturdy hands,
he struck the Gyraean rock, and split it apart;
sentences.i: At once he seized his trident in his sturdy hands, struck the Gyraean rock, and split it in two;
sentences.n: τρίαιναν, ‘trident’, is Poseidon’s characteristic weapon. στιβαρῇσιν, ‘sturdy, strong’, describes his hands. Γυραίην πέτρην, ‘the Gyraean rock’, singular here, is the same disputed place-name as at 500. ἀπὸ...ἔσχισεν is tmesis for ἀπέσχισεν, ‘split off’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν αὐτόθι μεῖνε, τὸ δὲ τρύφος ἔμπεσε πόντῳ,
τῷ ῥ’ Αἴας τὸ πρῶτον ἐφεζόμενος μέγ’ ἀάσθη·
sentences.tr:
kai to men autothi meine, to de tryphos empese pontōi,
tōi rh’ Aias to prōton ephezomenos meg’ aasthē·
sentences.l:
And the one part remained there, but the other piece fell into the sea,
on which Ajax, sitting at first, had been greatly blinded;
sentences.i: One part stayed where it was, but the broken piece fell into the sea — the very rock Ajax was sitting on when he was first struck with a great blindness of mind;
sentences.n: τρύφος, ‘a broken piece, fragment’, is a rare noun. ἐφεζόμενος is the present participle of ἐφέζομαι, ‘sit upon’. μέγ’ ἀάσθη repeats line 503 verbatim, describing the same reckless boast, and keeps the identical English, ‘greatly blinded’/‘a great blindness of mind’, as fixed there.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐφόρει κατὰ πόντον ἀπείρονα κυμαίνοντα.
sentences.tr: ton d’ ephorei kata ponton apeirona kymainonta.
sentences.l: and it bore him down through the boundless sea, as it heaved and surged.
sentences.i: and the sea, boundless and heaving, carried him down under its waves.
sentences.n: ἐφόρει, an imperfect of φορέω, describes him being swept along over time. ἀπείρονα, ‘boundless, endless’, and κυμαίνοντα, ‘surging, billowing’ (from κῦμα ‘wave’), both agree with πόντον, the object of κατά; the unstated subject of ἐφόρει is naturally the sea itself.

sentences.t: ὣς ὁ μὲν ἔνθ’ ἀπόλωλεν, ἐπεὶ πίεν ἁλμυρὸν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr: hōs ho men enth’ apolōlen, epei pien halmyron hydōr.
sentences.l: So he perished there, when he had drunk the briny water.
sentences.i: So he died there, after he had swallowed the salt water.
sentences.n: ἀπόλωλεν, a perfect of ἀπόλλυμι with vivid narrative force, ‘has perished, is dead’. πίεν is an unaugmented aorist of πίνω (Attic ἔπιε). This closes the Ajax episode within Proteus’s still-open speech.

sentences.t:
σὸς δέ που ἔκφυγε κῆρας ἀδελφεὸς ἠδ’ ὑπάλυξεν
ἐν νηυσὶ γλαφυρῇσι·
sentences.tr:
sos de pou ekphyge kēras adelpheos ēd’ hypalyxen
en nēusi glaphyrēisi·
sentences.l:
And your brother, I think, escaped the fates, and got clear away
in his hollow ships;
sentences.i: As for your brother, I believe he escaped the fates and got away safely in his hollow ships;
sentences.n: This unit begins a new paragraph in Murray’s text, turning from Ajax’s story to Agamemnon’s, but it remains inside Proteus’s still-open third speech, so — like the paragraph-break at 499, and the precedent at odyssey-017’s line 351 — it carries no mark and no quotation-reopening character. σὸς...ἀδελφεός, ‘your brother’, is Agamemnon. που, ‘I suppose’, is the same conjectural particle used at 498. ὑπάλυξεν is an aorist of ὑπαλύσκω, ‘slip away from, escape’. γλαφυρῇσι, ‘hollow’ (of ships), is the already-fixed epithet.

sentences.t: σάωσε δὲ πότνια Ἥρη.
sentences.tr: saōse de potnia Hērē.
sentences.l: and the lady Hera saved him.
sentences.i: for the lady Hera kept him safe.
sentences.n: σάωσε repeats the verb of line 444. πότνια, ‘lady, mistress’, is a title of respect for a goddess, already used of Calypso (1.14). Hera’s hostility to Troy, assumed but not explained here, accounts for her favor to the Achaean king.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τάχ’ ἔμελλε Μαλειάων ὄρος αἰπὺ
ἵξεσθαι,
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē tach’ emelle Maleiaōn oros aipy
hixesthai,
sentences.l:
But when he was soon about to reach
the steep mountain of Malea,
sentences.i: But when he was on the point of reaching the steep headland of Malea,
sentences.n: ἔμελλε with the infinitive ἵξεσθαι means ‘was about to, was on the verge of’. Μαλειάων...ὄρος αἰπύ names the notoriously dangerous headland at the southeastern tip of the Peloponnese; αἰπύς, ‘steep, sheer’, is the same adjective already fixed in αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος, here used of an actual height.

sentences.t:
τότε δή μιν ἀναρπάξασα θύελλα
πόντον ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντα φέρεν βαρέα στενάχοντα,
ἀγροῦ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιήν, ὅθι δώματα ναῖε Θυέστης
τὸ πρίν, ἀτὰρ τότ’ ἔναιε Θυεστιάδης Αἴγισθος.
sentences.tr:
tote dē min anarpaxasa thyella
ponton ep’ ichthyoenta pheren barea stenachonta,
agrou ep’ eschatiēn, hothi dōmata naie Thyestēs
to prin, atar tot’ enaie Thyestiadēs Aigisthos.
sentences.l:
then indeed a storm-blast, snatching him up,
bore him, groaning heavily, over the fish-teeming sea,
to the edge of the farmland, where Thyestes used to dwell in his house
before, but where then Aegisthus, son of Thyestes, was dwelling.
sentences.i: then a sudden storm-blast caught him up and carried him off, groaning heavily, across the fish-teeming sea, to the edge of the farmland where Thyestes used to live, but where Aegisthus, son of Thyestes, was living at that time.
sentences.n: ἀναρπάξασα, the aorist participle of ἀναρπάζω ‘snatch up’, agrees with θύελλα, ‘a storm-blast, squall’. πόντον...ἰχθυόεντα is the already-fixed ‘the fish-teeming sea’. ἐσχατιήν, ‘the edge, border’ of cultivated land. Θυεστιάδης, ‘son of Thyestes’, is a patronymic for Aegisthus; the family feud between Atreus and Thyestes is assumed known to the audience and is not narrated here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ καὶ κεῖθεν ἐφαίνετο νόστος ἀπήμων,
ἂψ δὲ θεοὶ οὖρον στρέψαν, καὶ οἴκαδ’ ἵκοντο,
ἦ τοι ὁ μὲν χαίρων ἐπεβήσετο πατρίδος αἴης
καὶ κύνει ἁπτόμενος ἣν πατρίδα·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē kai keithen ephaineto nostos apēmōn,
aps de theoi ouron strepsan, kai oikad’ hikonto,
ē toi ho men chairōn epebēseto patridos aiēs
kai kynei haptomenos hēn patrida·
sentences.l:
But when from there too a safe return home was appearing,
and the gods turned the wind back again, and they reached home,
then indeed he, rejoicing, set foot upon his native land,
and kissed it, laying hold of his own fatherland;
sentences.i: But when from there too a safe homecoming at last seemed near, and the gods turned the wind around again, and they reached home, Agamemnon set foot on his native soil rejoicing, and took hold of his own land and kissed it;
sentences.n: ἀπήμων, ‘safe, unharmed’, repeats line 487. στρέψαν is an unaugmented aorist of στρέφω. ἐπεβήσετο is an aorist middle of ἐπιβαίνω, ‘set foot upon’, governing the genitive. κύνει is the imperfect of κυνέω, ‘kiss’; ἁπτόμενος, ‘taking hold of’, governs the genitive.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δ’ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ
δάκρυα θερμὰ χέοντ’, ἐπεὶ ἀσπασίως ἴδε γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
polla d’ ap’ autou
dakrya therma cheont’, epei aspasiōs ide gaian.
sentences.l:
and many hot tears
were falling from him, since gladly he saw his land.
sentences.i: and many hot tears streamed down from him, so gladly did he look upon his land.
sentences.n: χέοντ(ο), an imperfect middle of χέω ‘pour, shed’, is the same verb behind the already-fixed δάκρυ χέων, ‘shedding tears’, here in the plural middle. ἀσπασίως, ‘gladly, joyfully’, is an adverb from ἀσπάσιος. ἴδε is an unaugmented aorist of ὁράω (= εἶδε).

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ἀπὸ σκοπιῆς εἶδε σκοπός, ὅν ῥα καθεῖσεν
Αἴγισθος δολόμητις ἄγων, ὑπὸ δ’ ἔσχετο μισθὸν
χρυσοῦ δοιὰ τάλαντα·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ar’ apo skopiēs eide skopos, hon rha katheisen
Aigisthos dolomētis agōn, hypo d’ escheto misthon
chrysou doia talanta·
sentences.i: But a watchman, whom Aegisthus of guileful counsel had brought and posted on a lookout, caught sight of him from his post, and Aegisthus had promised him as his wage two talents of gold;
sentences.n: σκοπιῆς...σκοπός, ‘a watch-post...a watchman’, repeats the same root deliberately. καθεῖσεν is the aorist of καθίζω, ‘set, station’. Αἴγισθος δολόμητις, ‘Aegisthus of guileful counsel’, is the already-fixed house epithet. ὑπὸ...ἔσχετο is tmesis for ὑπέσχετο, the aorist of ὑπισχνέομαι, ‘promise’. A τάλαντον is a unit of weight for precious metal.

sentences.t:
φύλασσε δ’ ὅ γ’ εἰς ἐνιαυτόν,
μή ἑ λάθοι παριών, μνήσαιτο δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.tr:
phylasse d’ ho g’ eis eniauton,
mē he lathoi pariōn, mnēsaito de thouridos alkēs.
sentences.l:
And he kept watch for a full year,
lest he should pass by unnoticed, and might remember his impetuous might.
sentences.i: And the watchman kept watch for a whole year, so that Agamemnon should not slip past him unnoticed, and so that Aegisthus might call his own furious courage to mind in time.
sentences.n: φύλασσε is the imperfect of φυλάσσω, ‘keep watch’. λάθοι is an optative of λανθάνω, ‘escape notice’. μνήσαιτο is an optative of μιμνήσκομαι, ‘call to mind’. θούριδος ἀλκῆς, ‘impetuous might, furious valor’ (θοῦρις + ἀλκή), is a standing Homeric phrase for warlike vigor, here what Aegisthus must nerve himself to use.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν ἀγγελέων πρὸς δώματα ποιμένι λαῶν.
sentences.tr: bē d’ imen angeleōn pros dōmata poimeni laōn.
sentences.l: And he set out to go, bringing word, to the halls, to the shepherd of the people.
sentences.i: So the watchman set out for the halls to bring word to the shepherd of the people.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεν, ‘he set out to go’, is the already-fixed formula. ἀγγελέων, a future participle of ἀγγέλλω, expresses purpose, ‘to bring news’. ποιμένι λαῶν, ‘shepherd of the people’, the already-fixed epithet, is used here of Aegisthus himself, in his role as the local master where he has installed himself — not of Agamemnon, who is still on his way.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα δ’ Αἴγισθος δολίην ἐφράσσατο τέχνην·
sentences.tr: autika d’ Aigisthos doliēn ephrassato technēn·
sentences.l: And at once Aegisthus devised a guileful device;
sentences.i: At once Aegisthus devised a guileful device of his own;
sentences.n: δολίην...τέχνην, ‘a guileful device’, repeats the exact collocation already used of Proteus’s shape-shifting skill at 455 (δολίης...τέχνης); the same English is kept for both, since Homer’s reuse of the identical phrase draws a pointed parallel between the Old Man’s guileful craft and Aegisthus’s guileful plot — see new-renderings.md. ἐφράσσατο, ‘devised, contrived’, is the same verb used of Eidothea’s remedy at 444.

sentences.t:
κρινάμενος κατὰ δῆμον ἐείκοσι φῶτας ἀρίστους
εἷσε λόχον, ἑτέρωθι δ’ ἀνώγει δαῖτα πένεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
krinamenos kata dēmon eeikosi phōtas aristous
heise lochon, heterōthi d’ anōgei daita penesthai.
sentences.l:
having chosen throughout the district twenty of the best men,
he set an ambush, and elsewhere he ordered a feast to be prepared.
sentences.i: He picked out twenty of the best men in the district, set them in ambush, and meanwhile ordered a feast to be got ready elsewhere.
sentences.n: κρινάμενος is the aorist middle participle of κρίνω, ‘pick out, choose’. εἷσε, the aorist of ἵζω, is causative, ‘set, stationed’. ἑτέρωθι, ‘elsewhere’, marks the double trap: an ambush in one place, a decoy feast in another. ἀνώγει is an imperfect of ἄνωγα, ‘was ordering, bade’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ βῆ καλέων Ἀγαμέμνονα, ποιμένα λαῶν
ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν, ἀεικέα μερμηρίζων.
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē kaleōn Agamemnona, poimena laōn
hippoisin kai ochesphin, aeikea mermērizōn.
sentences.l:
But he himself went, calling Agamemnon, shepherd of the people,
with horses and chariot, pondering unseemly things.
sentences.i: But Aegisthus himself went with horses and a chariot to invite Agamemnon, shepherd of the people, brooding on his ugly plan.
sentences.n: ποιμένα λαῶν, ‘shepherd of the people’, the already-fixed epithet, here names Agamemnon himself, being summoned to his death. ὄχεσφιν is a dative/instrumental plural in the old case-suffix -φι of ὄχος, ‘chariot’. ἀεικέα μερμηρίζων, ‘pondering unseemly things’, uses the same adjective ἀεικής already fixed in ἀεικέα πότμον, ‘an unseemly doom’, here substantival of the murder Aegisthus has in mind.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ οὐκ εἰδότ’ ὄλεθρον ἀνήγαγε καὶ κατέπεφνεν
δειπνίσσας, ὥς τίς τε κατέκτανε βοῦν ἐπὶ φάτνῃ.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ouk eidot’ olethron anēgage kai katepephnen
deipnissas, hōs tis te katektane boun epi phatnēi.
sentences.l:
And him, not knowing his doom, he led up and slew,
having feasted him, as one slays an ox at the manger.
sentences.i: He led him up, unaware of the death awaiting him, feasted him, and killed him, as one might slaughter an ox at its manger.
sentences.n: εἰδότ(α), a perfect participle of οἶδα with present force, means ‘not knowing’. ἀνήγαγε is the aorist of ἀνάγω, ‘lead up (to the house)’. κατέπεφνεν is an old reduplicated aorist meaning ‘slew’, from the same stem as πεφνεῖν. δειπνίσσας, ‘having feasted’, is from δειπνίζω. The simile of the ox at the manger reduces the murder to plain butchery.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις Ἀτρεΐδεω ἑτάρων λίπεθ’ οἵ οἱ ἕποντο,
οὐδέ τις Αἰγίσθου, ἀλλ’ ἔκταθεν ἐν μεγάροισιν.
sentences.tr:
oude tis Atreïdeō hetarōn lipeth’ hoi hoi heponto,
oude tis Aigisthou, all’ ektathen en megaroisin.
sentences.l:
Nor was anyone of the son of Atreus’ companions left, who followed him,
nor anyone of Aegisthus’s men, but they were slain in the halls.
sentences.i: Not one of the son of Atreus’s companions who had followed him was left alive, nor one of Aegisthus’s men either — all were cut down together in the halls.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδεω is a genitive in -εω of Ἀτρεΐδης (= Attic Ἀτρείδου), ‘of the son of Atreus’, kept as the fixed periphrasis for Agamemnon rather than naming him, since the Greek withholds the name here. ἔκταθεν is a passive aorist form of κτείνω, ‘were slain’; its augment status is left undescribed for want of certainty. Proteus’s third speech does not close within this part: the famous continuation of the story, Orestes’ revenge on Aegisthus, follows immediately in the poem beyond line 537, so no closing quotation mark is given here.
